study.title: 1 Corinthians 5 Discipline, purity, and testimony of the church
study.overview: Paul deals with a serious sexual sin within the church and censors the proud tolerance of the Corinthians. He commands the community to act with mourning, discipline, and exclusion from persistent sin, not because Christians should isolate themselves from the world, but because the church needs to keep its holiness. The chapter connects discipline and restoration: correction aims at the destruction of the flesh, that is, of sinful impulse, so that one can be saved in the Lord's day. At the same time, Paul distinguishes between judging the inside and outside, leaving the final judgment from outside to God.

outline.title: Public scandal and pride of the church
outline.explanation: Paul denounces such a serious case of sexual immorality that neither the outside people approved it. The church, instead of grief, was proud; therefore, should remove from the midst of it the stubborn practitioner of this sin.

outline.title: Apostolic Judgment, Discipline and Paschal Holiness
outline.explanation: Even physically absent, Paul has already pronounced his judgment in the name and with the power of Christ: man should be delivered to Satan, so that the "carne is destroyed and the spirit was saved." The apostle uses the image of the leaven to show that a tolerated sin defileth the whole community, and relates the purity of the church to Christ, our Passover, sacrificed for us.

outline.title: Separation of internal sin and pastoral responsibility
outline.explanation: Paul clarifies that he did not want a total separation from the sinners of the world, for this would require leaving the world. The point is not to maintain communion of table and spiritual recognition with whom, saying brother, lives in notorious sin and without repentance. The church must judge its own; God will judge them from outside.

study.context: The notes indicate that Paul had previously written guidance on not associating with sexually immoral people, although there is discussion whether this refers to a lost letter or instructions already given in this same epistle. The chapter also parallels the easter and leaven, a language that helps Paul speak of community cleanliness and new life. There is no, in the notes, safe data beyond that on dates, geography or external circumstances.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that the holiness of the church is not optional. Grace does not eliminate discipline; rather, it makes it necessary when there is public and obstinate sin among those who say themselves brothers. Paul does not treat discipline as revenge, but as a corrective measure and even redemptive: the goal is the final salvation of the person and the preservation of the community. The metaphor of leaven shows that sin is not only individual, for it spreads and corrupts the whole body. The reference to Christ, our passover, gives Christological foundation to purity: whoever was attained by the sacrifice of Christ must live as a people separated from the old leaven. There is also an important distinction between internal discipline and the judgment of those from outside: the church responds by its professed members, while the final judgment of those from outside belongs to God.

scholarViews.insight: The surrender is understood as an exclusion from the protection of the church and exposure to the dominion of the evil one, with a corrective and perhaps restorative purpose, so that the spirit may be saved in the Lord's day.
The "old leaven" can represent the need for the church to purify itself by removing the scandalous member, so that it may be a new and holy mass before God.
Paul does not command to judge those from outside as if they were members of the church; they are not under the same discipline and their judgment belongs to God.

questions: Why does Paul consider the church's tolerance so serious before this open sin?
How does the image of leaven help to understand the effect of sin on the Christian community?
How can the discipline of the church seek restoration rather than mere punishment?
study.practice: The church and every believer should examine whether they are normalizing sins that God calls to abandon. When there is a serious and persistent sin among those who confess faith, the right answer is neither pride nor indifference, but sadness, truth and responsible pastoral action. It is also necessary to distinguish between correcting brothers and condemning those from outside: we must witness to the world without assuming the place of final judgment, and maintain Christian communion marked by sincerity and truth.
study.uncertainty: The notes do not allow us to state with certainty whether the letter mentioned in 1 Corinthians 5:9 was a today lost epistle or reference to instructions already written in this same letter. Nor is there sufficient basis, in the given notes, to define in a dogmatic way whether to deliver Satan's disease, extraordinary affliction, formal excommunication or a combination of these ideas; however, the central meaning, however, is severe discipline with corrective purpose.
